claims.text: The starting alloy is an as-cast, nominally single-phase high-entropy alloy with a fully chemically disordered random distribution of constituent atoms.
Controlled annealing can promote short-range chemical ordering without causing macroscopic phase segregation in this alloy.
The annealing treatment produces enhanced nanometer-scale clustering of specific element pairs.
Short-range chemical order reduces the random lattice-potential landscape.
Reduced random potential fluctuations decrease the electron-scattering rate.
The reduction in electron scattering improves electron–phonon coupling.
Enhanced local chemical ordering decreases the effective Coulomb repulsion.
Improved electron–phonon coupling and reduced effective Coulomb repulsion enable Cooper-pair formation at low temperature.
The annealed alloy will exhibit a superconducting transition below a well-defined critical temperature.
The predicted superconducting transition will produce a sharp drop in electrical resistivity and the onset of diamagnetic susceptibility.
Excessive disorder-induced scattering suppresses superconductivity in the as-cast baseline.
The as-cast baseline will show no measurable superconducting transition or a substantially depressed critical temperature.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply only while annealing produces local short-range order without large-scale phase segregation.
The proposed mechanism applies in the approximate temperature range of 0–10 K.
Formation of a multiphase state may eliminate the predicted enhancement of superconductivity.
